title: The Gamble
body:
The Gamble

ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते ।
सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ।।

"While contemplating the objects of the senses, one develops an attachment to them. Attachment leads to desire, and from desire arises anger. (Gita II-62)"

The extraordinary prosperity of Indraprastha and the imperial status of Yudhishthira was more than Duryodhana's envious heart could tolerate. Day by day, Duryodhana pined away in jealousy, his mind consumed by Mayasura's palace of illusions where he had once mistaken solid crystal for a pool of water, earning the laughter of Draupadi. To strip Yudhishthira of his wealth without a bloody military campaign, Shakuni suggested a cunning plan: inviting Yudhishthira to a game of dice, utilizing his well-known weakness for play and Shakuni's absolute mastery of deceitful throws.
Dhritarashtra reluctantly gave his assent, choosing to override the solemn, protective warnings of Vidura. When Vidura arrived in Indraprastha to deliver the formal invitation, he openly cautioned Yudhishthira that the match was a calculated trap designed to bring about the ruin of their house. Yet, Yudhishthira accepted, bound by the Kshatriya code of honor that made it a matter of absolute shame to reject a formal challenge, and further driven by an inner, unvanquished attachment to the game.
In the royal hall of Hastinapur, in the presence of Bheeshma, Drona, Kripa, and Vidura, the tragic game commenced. Shakuni cast the dice on behalf of Duryodhana, using bone dice that obeyed his mental commands. In rapid, agonizing succession, Yudhishthira wagered and lost his gold, his silver, his vast stables, his armies, and his servants. Blinded by the fever of the game and refusing to halt, he wagered and lost his brothers Nakula, Sahadeva, Arjuna, and Bhima. Finally, Yudhishthira staked his own freedom, falling into absolute bondage as Shakuni shouted his triumphant cry: 'I have won!'
